2.text: The tale proceeds to describe how the scabby orphan, under the protection

3.text: of the Merciful Being, became a very strong, good-looking young man. He

4.text: found much wealth, and at last married a young, pretty girl.

5.text: Then those who had but recently practised violence on him, came and

6.text: said, each of them, “You are my nephew, you are my cousin.” But he

7.text: pushed them away and answered, “I am not yours, I am a stranger. I am

8.text: an orphan. You have beaten me all the time.”

9.text: Then he and his wife left the village altogether, and went to another

10.text: place. The people of the village, however, were unsuccessful in hunting, and

11.text: could find no food. The marrow of their bones was all dried up; and soon

12.text: they died, every one of them. The orphan founded a living-place, and his

13.text: family increased in number and became a village.¹

23.text: The tales of the Reindeer Chukchee, when describing an orphan, represent

24.text: him as persecuted by a step-mother in his own family. He leaves his camp

25.text: and wanders among the neighboring camps as an “idle wanderer,” or goes

26.text: away to a distant country in search of a fortune. The social life of the Rein-

27.text: deer people evidently has no place for him in his native land.

28.text: Various authors, when describing the social life of the American Eskimo,

29.text: mention with praise their friendliness to those not able to provide for them-

30.text: selves. Hans Egede says, “They do not let those people starve, but admit

31.text: them freely to their table.”³ Dr. Franz Boas says of the Central Eskimo

32.text: that poor men are adopted by strange families. Particularly bachelors without

33.text: any relatives, cripples who are not able to provide for themselves, or men

34.text: who have lost their sledges and dogs, are found in this position. Nor are

35.text: these men less esteemed than the self-dependent providers.⁴ All this presents

36.text: great similarity to the customs of the Maritime Chukchee. Still it would seem

37.text: that the consideration of the Maritime Chukchee for their poor does not extend

38.text: so far as it does among the American Eskimo.
